entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Liu Yiqing (403–444 CE), Prince of Linchuan and nephew of Emperor Wu of Liu Song, was a pivotal figure in the cultural and intellectual life of the Southern Dynasties, particularly renowned for his patronage of scholarship and compilation of the *Shishuo Xinyu* (A New Account of Tales of the World). Born in Xuzhou, he navigated the tumultuous political landscape of the early Liu Song dynasty, serving in various high-ranking official positions, including Governor of Jingzhou and Jiangzhou, before ultimately settling into a life of literary and historical pursuit. His efforts provided a unique window into the aristocratic society and intellectual currents of 5th-century China, preserving anecdotes, conversations, and character sketches of prominent individuals from the late Han to the Eastern Jin dynasties.

His most enduring contribution, the *Shishuo Xinyu*, completed around 430 CE, is an unparalleled collection of approximately 1,130 short anecdotes organized into 36 chapters by topic, such as 'Speech and Conversation,' 'Literature,' and 'Admonitions and Remonstrances.' This work, compiled with the assistance of a team of literati, including He Chong and Yuan Shu, meticulously records the wit, eccentricities, and moral dilemmas of the gentry class, particularly those associated with the 'pure conversation' (qingtan) movement. It serves not only as a historical document but also as a literary masterpiece, capturing the spirit of an age characterized by intellectual ferment, philosophical inquiry, and the flourishing of distinctive aristocratic culture, often under the shadow of political instability and inter-dynastic conflict.

Its preservation of aristocratic anecdotes offers unique insights into a pivotal era of Chinese history.
